qs.q: An infant is diagnosed with tetralogy of Fallot, characterized by pulmonary stenosis, ventricular septal defect, overriding aorta, and right ventricular hypertrophy. A single developmental error explains this constellation; what is it?
o: Primary agenesis of the superior endocardial cushion
Unequal asymmetric division of the truncus arteriosus
Failure of the septum secundum to cover the foramen
Complete absence of the embryonic sinus venosus horn
Premature closure of the fetal ductus arteriosus vessel
qs.e: Unequal division of the truncus arteriosus by the aortopulmonary septum causes both pulmonary stenosis and the VSD.
qs.s: Weekly Year 1: Embryology Exam - October 30, 2026 (Section A: MCQs)

qs.q: A 3-year-old child with a large, unrepaired ventricular septal defect develops Eisenmenger's syndrome. What primary physiological alteration characterizes this complication?
o: Spontaneous closure of the septal defect with resolution of heart failure
Marked reduction in pulmonary vascular resistance elevating the Qp:Qs ratio
Severe systemic hypotension driven by excessive peripheral afterload drop
Reversal of the shunt to right-to-left causing progressive central cyanosis
qs.e: Eisenmenger's syndrome occurs when chronic left-to-right shunting causes severe pulmonary vascular disease and pulmonary hypertension, eventually reversing the shunt to right-to-left. This process involves irreversible pulmonary vascular remodeling rather than a drop in resistance or spontaneous defect closure.

qs.q: Surgical closure of a complete ventricular septal defect is usually performed before what age to prevent Eisenmenger syndrome?
o: One year of age
Five years of age
Six months of age
Two years of age
qs.e: Early repair (<6 months) avoids the development of Eisenmenger. Delaying beyond 1 year increases the risk.

qs.q: What is the definitive, appropriate surgical management for a child with a very large ventricular septal defect (VSD)?
o: Close monitoring for possible spontaneous closure
Palliative care provided for inoperable condition
Open‑heart patch closure using cardiopulmonary bypass
Primary suture repair performed under tension
qs.e: Very large VSDs require open-heart surgery with patch closure under cardiopulmonary bypass to prevent complications like heart failure and pulmonary hypertension. Monitoring closely is reserved for small, restrictive defects that have a high likelihood of spontaneous closure.

qs.q: A 3-year-old with a ventricular septal defect (VSD) initially had left-to-right shunting. One year later, the child presents with cyanosis and right-to-left shunting. What is this phenomenon called?
o: Cor pulmonale
Tet spell
Eisenmenger syndrome
Blalock-Taussig shunt
qs.e: The reversal of shunt direction from left-to-right to right-to-left in a long-standing VSD is known as Eisenmenger syndrome. Cor pulmonale refers to right heart failure, not the shunt reversal itself.

qs.q: A 6-month-old infant with a large, uncorrected ventricular septal defect undergoes echocardiography to assess cardiac remodeling. Which of the following sets of cardiac chambers is expected to show the greatest dilation?
o: Right atrium and right ventricle
Right atrium and left ventricle
Left atrium and right ventricle
Left atrium and left ventricle
qs.e: A left-to-right shunt at the ventricular level causes chronic volume overload resulting in dilation of the left atrium and left ventricle. In contrast, atrial-level shunts predominantly dilate the right-sided chambers.

qs.q: A 3-week-old infant with a moderate-sized ventricular septal defect has a normal physical examination without murmurs or signs of heart failure. Why do infants with this defect typically lack symptoms during the first few weeks of life?
o: The shunt orifice has not yet reached critical size
The ductus arteriosus temporarily masks the defect
Immediate closure of the foramen ovale limits flow
High fetal pulmonary vascular resistance limits the shunt
qs.e: High pulmonary vascular resistance in the first weeks of life limits the left-to-right shunt, delaying symptoms and murmurs until resistance drops around 4 to 8 weeks. Lower resistance would typically cause early manifestations of heart failure.

qs.q: Most ventricular septal defects (VSDs) occur in which part of the septum?
o: Lower septum
Membranous part
Muscular part
Infundibular part
qs.e: The membranous part of the ventricular septum is the most common site for VSDs.

ai.title: Ventricular Septal Defect
ai.subject: Paediatrics
ai.summary: A VSD is a hole in the ventricular septum causing left-to-right shunt. Clinical focus is on size, haemodynamic impact and risk of Eisenmenger. Management balances observation, medical therapy and timely surgery.

sections.p: A VSD is an opening in the interventricular septum allowing blood to flow from the high‑pressure left ventricle to the right ventricle during systole. Diagnosis is clinical plus echocardiography; ECG and chest X‑ray support the assessment.
b: Pansystolic murmur at left lower sternal edge
Echocardiography shows defect size, location and shunt direction

t.b: Shows septal anatomy, flow velocity, Qp:Qs ratio; guides management
Enlarged cardiac silhouette indicates significant left‑to‑right shunt
Right‑ventricular strain pattern suggests large VSD

sections.p: Severity is graded by shunt magnitude (Qp:Qs) and clinical impact. Small VSDs (Qp:Qs<1.5) often close spontaneously. Moderate (1.5–2.5) may need intervention; large (>2.5) risk heart failure and Eisenmenger.
Most VSDs are sporadic, but consider maternal rubella, diabetes, alcohol, and teratogens. In low‑resource settings, infections (e.g., HIV, TB) and nutritional deficiencies may increase risk.
Typical features include a harsh pansystolic murmur, bounding pulses, and a wide pulse pressure. Large defects cause failure to thrive, tachypnoea, and recurrent infections.
b: Pansystolic murmur at left lower sternal edge

sections.p: Echocardiography is the gold standard. In settings without echo, a bedside Doppler or pulse oximetry may give clues. Lab tests rule out infections.

t.b: Normal in left‑to‑right shunt; low in Eisenmenger
Leucocytosis suggests infection; anaemia may worsen symptoms

sections.p: Urgent signs include severe dyspnoea, cardiomegaly, pulmonary hypertension, and cyanosis. Complications are heart failure, arrhythmia, infective endocarditis, and Eisenmenger syndrome.

Treat underlying causes, provide supportive care (oxygen, diuretics, ACE inhibitors), and plan surgical closure for large or symptomatic defects. Medical therapy is reserved for small, asymptomatic VSDs.

t.b: Reduce afterload and LV volume overload
Symptomatic fluid overload or pulmonary congestion

sections.p: Regular echocardiograms every 6–12 months for moderate VSDs. Counsel parents on infection prevention and avoid herbal remedies that may worsen haemodynamics.
Large VSD mimics aortic regurgitation or tricuspid regurgitation. A pansystolic murmur can also be due to mitral regurgitation.
A normal chest X‑ray does not exclude a moderate VSD; small defects may be missed. Pulse oximetry may remain normal until pulmonary hypertension develops.
b: Normal chest X‑ray in moderate VSD

faq.q: What is the most common type of VSD?
faq.a: Membranous VSD is the most frequent, located near the aortic and pulmonary valves.

faq.q: Can a VSD close on its own?
faq.a: Yes, small VSDs (<5 mm) often close spontaneously within the first year of life.

faq.q: Why is infective endocarditis prophylaxis recommended?
faq.a: Large VSDs expose the endocardium to high shear stress, increasing risk of bacterial colonisation during invasive procedures.

exam: A 2‑year‑old presents with tachypnoea and a harsh pansystolic murmur at the left lower sternal edge. What is the next best investigation? — Echocardiography to assess defect size and shunt magnitude.
A child with a known VSD develops cyanosis and clubbing. What complication is most likely? — Eisenmenger syndrome due to reversed shunt.
During a routine exam you hear a pansystolic murmur at the apex radiating to the axilla. What is the most likely diagnosis? — Mitral regurgitation, not VSD.
A 6‑month‑old with a small VSD is asymptomatic. What is the recommended management? — Observation with serial echocardiograms; no surgery needed.

A patient with a large VSD is started on diuretics. Which drug class is contraindicated in this setting? — Loop diuretics are fine; however, NSAIDs should be avoided due to risk of renal impairment and reduced diuretic efficacy.
A VSD patient is scheduled for surgery but has active malaria infection. What should be done? — Treat malaria first and delay surgery until infection resolves.
